# A Conspiracy of Lichens

There is a granite marker in the cemetery up the hill from my house, raised for somebody born in the 1830s, and the oldest part of the inscription has gone soft. The stone itself is legible where the rain washes it, but across the upper third, where the moss keeps to itself and the sun barely reaches, the letters have been colonized by pale green rings that overlap like a map of forgotten countries. Whoever is buried there has been dead for over a century, and for most of that century something alive has been reading the stone, millimeter by millimeter, in complete silence.

Nobody goes anywhere to look at lichens. Nobody plans a vacation around them, writes songs about them, keeps them as pets. That is, in a way, their whole strategy. While everything else in the living world shouts — bright petals, loud birds, the whole carnival of obvious life — the lichens practice a kind of radical modesty. They are gray, green-gray, crust-white, sometimes a startling orange or a whisper of yellow, and they grow on rocks, roofs, tombstones, tree bark, fence posts, the baked soil of deserts, the bare stone of Antarctica. By some estimates they cover something like six percent of the land surface of the Earth. You have walked past a few thousand of them today without a single thought. They were here before the continents took their current shapes, in some form, and they will very likely be here after we are a subject for paleontologists.

The first thing to understand about a lichen is that it is not a plant. It is not, strictly speaking, an organism at all — or rather, it is an organism the way a married couple is a single person. A lichen is a partnership: a fungus, which is more closely related to animals than to plants, and an alga or a cyanobacterium, which can photosynthesize. The fungus builds the house — the tough, layered body you actually see — and the alga lives inside it, paying rent in sugar manufactured from light and air. The Canadian lichenologist Trevor Goward put it in a sentence that has become the field's unofficial motto: lichens are fungi that have discovered agriculture. The fungus farms. The crop is sunshine.

When the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed this in 1867, he was treated as a crank. The idea was called "the dual hypothesis," and its opponents coined a sneering label for Schwendener's supporters — the Sensationalists — on the theory that he had invented a sensational story to explain away an inconvenient puzzle. The scandal wasn't really about lichens. It was about categories. Nineteenth-century biology had worked very hard to sort the living world into clean, dignified boxes, and here was Schwendener insisting that one of the most common sights on Earth was a box containing two things that officially belonged in different kingdoms. It took decades of microscopy to settle it, but settle it it did: the lichen is a double act, classified by its fungal partner, and there are something like twenty thousand known kinds of it, each one a different arrangement of the same ancient deal.

And then, in 2016, the deal got more complicated. A lichenologist named Toby Spribille was studying the horsehair lichens of the Pacific Northwest — dark, wiry things that drape the branches of old forests and that flying squirrels and mountain caribou browse through the winter. Two species in this group looked nearly identical under the microscope, and in some cases even shared the same fungal DNA, yet produced different chemistry, one kind carrying a compound the other lacked. Nobody could explain it. Spribille, working with collaborators, ran a survey of all the genetic material inside these lichens and found something nobody had thought to look for: a third partner. A yeast — a basidiomycete, a distant cousin of baker's yeast — living embedded in the outer layer of the lichen's body, present in one lineage and absent in the other, correlated with the chemical difference. The lichens were not double acts after all. They were trios, at minimum.

There is a human story folded into that discovery, and it's worth telling. Spribille grew up in Montana, was homeschooled in a way that never quite produced a high school diploma, taught himself botany in the field, and eventually found his way to a doctorate in Austria — a path so unusual that when his paper came out in *Science*, a great deal of the coverage was about the man as much as the yeast. And his first reaction to his own result was disbelief. He assumed the yeast signal was contamination, a lab error, and spent months trying to disprove his own discovery before conceding that the third partner was real. Which is the honest way to do science, and also the hardest. What his finding meant for the field was almost philosophical: the paradigm that had taken a century and a half to accept — lichen = fungus + alga — was itself an oversimplification. The thing we had finally agreed to call a partnership of two was actually a partnership of two, plus whoever else had been quietly invited and never introduced. A lichen is not a noun doing the work of a sentence. It is a committee with an extremely low turnover rate.

The committee has powers that no individual member has alone, and some of those powers are absurd. Consider drought. A lichen has no roots, no way to store water, no protection worth the name. When its environment dries out — which can be for weeks, months, years — it does not fight the drought. It simply stops. Water content drops to almost nothing, metabolism winds down to a standstill, the whole structure hardens into something like dry paper and waits. Most organisms die in that condition. The lichen treats it as a Tuesday. Then the rain comes, and within minutes — minutes — photosynthesis restarts, the gray crust flushes faintly green, and the committee is back in session. It is hard to overstate how strange this is. Nearly every form of complex life we know is in a constant, desperate negotiation with dehydration. The lichen opted out of the negotiation centuries ago and never looked back.

This trick works even in open space. In 2005, European researchers strapped samples of two lichen species to the outside of an orbiting capsule and left them clamped to the hull, fully exposed, for about two weeks: hard vacuum, brutal temperature swings, the unfiltered ultraviolet of the sun with nothing between it and the cells. The lichens survived. Not in some protected, dormant corner — the most exposed samples fared oddly well. A later experiment left lichens outside the International Space Station for a year and a half. Again: they came back and resumed photosynthesis as though returning from a mildly dull holiday. No other macroscopic life form has demonstrated anything comparable. Tardigrades get the press, but a tardigrade is a speck with a strategy; a lichen is a visible, structured, functioning ecosystem, and it shrugged off the void.

Back on Earth, the committee's resume is just as strange. Lichens are the great pioneers, the ones who show up first at the rawest real estate on the planet — fresh lava, retreating glaciers, bare rock. They do it chemically: lichen acids slowly etch the stone itself, cracking minerals loose, while the body of the lichen traps drifting dust. Generations die and compress into the first proto-soil, a few grams of substrate in which mosses can take hold, then grasses, then everything else. Much of the soil under your feet began as lichen scratchwork on bare rock. In the deserts of the American Southwest, lichens are central players in the biological crusts that bind the soil and keep it from blowing away; stomp on a desert crust and you set back a community that may have taken centuries to assemble. In the boreal north, reindeer lichen — actually a lichen, despite the name — can constitute the majority of a caribou's winter diet, which means that wolves, in a very real sense, eat lichens at one remove. Humans have squeezed purple and red dyes out of them for centuries; the original litmus dye, the one behind every "litmus test" ever uttered, came from lichens. Oakmoss, a lichen, is a quiet staple of fine perfumery, one of the reasons classical fragrances smell like a forest floor after rain. You have almost certainly worn one, eaten traces of one, and benefited from one without ever noticing.

And they are slow. That is the other headline. A crustose lichen — the flat, painted-on kind — may expand on the order of a millimeter a year, sometimes a millimeter per decade. The map lichens of Greenland and the high Arctic grow so reliably slowly that geologists learned to use them as rulers: measure the largest lichen on a boulder, and you can estimate how long ago the ice released that boulder. The technique, lichenometry, has been dating glacial retreats since the 1950s. The same logic applies to the gravestone up the hill. The rings on the stone are a clock sitting on top of another clock, and by some estimates the oldest individual lichens on Earth — those patient Greenland map-circles — have been alive for something like four thousand years. A single connected patch of fungus and algae, older than most of the languages now spoken, older than the alphabet you are reading, quietly metabolizing on a rock.

Here is where the lichen stops being a curiosity and starts being an argument. For a long time, the official story of life was competition — Darwin's "war of nature," red tooth and claw, every organism against every other. And competition is real; nobody sane denies it. But the deeper you dig, the more the fundamental events of life's history turn out to be mergers. In the 1960s, a biologist named Lynn Margulis argued that the organelles inside complex cells — mitochondria, which power us; chloroplasts, which feed plants — were once free-living bacteria that moved inside other cells and stayed, evolving into permanent residents. Her paper was rejected by more than a dozen journals. The idea that the cell itself was an ancient coalition seemed too strange, too intimate. It is now textbook orthodoxy, proven in detail: your mitochondria still carry their own tiny genomes, molecular souvenirs of their independent lives, something like two billion years ago. Every cell in your body is a negotiated settlement of ancient microbes. The bacteria living in your gut outnumber your own cells roughly one to one, or close enough, and participate in your digestion, your immunity, possibly your moods. You are not contaminated by microbes. You are a collaborative of them, a lichen that learned to walk. The biologist who coined the word "symbiosis" in the 1870s defined it, remember, with deliberate neutrality: simply "living together." It was never meant to be a rare condition. It was meant to be the norm. The lichen, on its rock, is just the version of the norm you can see from a footpath.

There is a darker, more useful chapter too. Lichens are notoriously sensitive to air quality, because they have no skin, no waxy cuticle, no way to refuse what the air offers. They simply absorb it all. When industrial cities ran on coal, and sulfur dioxide hung over everything, lichens vanished across vast zones — nineteenth-century naturalists in London and Manchester noted the "lichen deserts" spreading around the smokestacks like stains in reverse. One species, though, tolerates sulfur beautifully: a gray-green crust called *Lecanora conizaeoides*, which spent the sootiest decades of the industrial era metastasizing across trees and walls, nearly alone in its kingdom, thriving on the poison that killed its neighbors. Then came clean air legislation, and the story reversed. Sensitive species crept back into the cities, and *L. conizaeoides*, the great beneficiary of the smog, began its long retreat. Lichens are now used deliberately, all over the world, as living instruments: survey crews read the walls and the bark the way a seismograph reads the ground. There is a pleasing symmetry in this. The original litmus test came from a lichen, and lichens remain, literally and figuratively, the litmus test — slow, honest sensors with no off switch, keeping a continuous record of what we have chosen to breathe.

So what do you do with all this, on an ordinary walk, past an ordinary stone? I keep turning over a few things. One is about time. We tend to treat slowness as failure — as the condition of things that couldn't hack it at our speed. The lichen suggests otherwise. Its slowness is not a deficit; it is the calibration that lets a being with no moving parts, no armor, and no way to run from anything persist through ice ages, droughts, and the vacuum of space. Speed is one survival strategy among many, and not obviously the most durable one. Another is about place. Lichens live at the margins — the cracks, the bark, the roof shingles, the tombstones, the "bare" rock where nothing worthwhile is supposedly happening. It turns out the margins are where soil gets made, where the frontier of the living world actually stands. Almost everything interesting in this story happened at an edge, in the spaces between categories, among organisms nobody bothered to look at.

And the deepest one is about identity. The lesson of the lichen is not exactly that cooperation beats competition. It's that the line between the two is drawn in pencil. A lichen is a partnership that behaves, for all purposes, as an individual — it has a name, a form, an ecological role, a life history. Underneath the name, it is a negotiation that has been running for hundreds of millions of years, successful enough that no one inside it bothers to keep score. The word "conspiracy" comes from Latin: *conspirare*, to breathe together. That is all a lichen has ever done — breathed together, two or three lineages sharing one small wet breath for an epoch. It is a strange comfort, somehow. The stone up the hill gives the lichen something to hold on to, and the lichen gives the stone someone to remember it by, and neither of them is in any hurry, and between them they have worked out something we are still struggling to put into words: that living things are not really things at all, but agreements — and that some agreements can outlast continents.
